description:
About Team THERMA

We are a team of four participants taking on NASA's Space Apps Challenge 2026, focusing on MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots: Harmonization.

Our goal is to explore how satellite-based thermal hotspot data can be harmonized to provide more consistent, meaningful, and accessible information about hotspots across Earth.

We are interested in Earth observation, space technology, data analysis, and software development.
summary: MODIS and VIIRS both detect active fires from orbit, but at different spatial resolutions: 1 km for MODIS, 375 m for VIIRS. As a result, the same fire event can produce very different hot-spot counts, which makes the two records hard to compare. THERMA harmonizes them onto a single, consistent scale. Drawing on NASA FIRMS, GWIS and INPE data, it builds a Burning Activity Calendar for nine fire-prone regions from 2016 to 2026. It also scores each month against a 2016–2025 baseline to flag anomalous fire activity, and gives a HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW likelihood rating for the next four months. Every rating states the rule and the number of baseline years behind it, and data gaps are flagged rather than hidden. The outcome is a transparent, comparable fire record that researchers and environmental groups can interpret with confidence.
details:
What it does and how it works
THERMA harmonizes active-fire detections from MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21). Because VIIRS works at 375 m resolution and MODIS at 1 km, VIIRS reports several detections where MODIS sees one, so THERMA converts both into a single comparable unit. The harmonized data feeds a Burning Activity Calendar covering nine fire-prone regions from 2016 to 2026: the Amazon, California, the Mediterranean EU-5, Chile, Portugal, Greece, Australia, Indonesia and Malaysia. Each month is scored against a 2016–2025 baseline, and months two or more standard deviations above normal are flagged as anomalies. A four-month outlook then rates the likelihood of above-normal fire as HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW, and states the rule and the number of baseline years behind each rating. The app also includes an interactive hot-spot map, a fire-spread model, weather, resource and containment planning, fire reports, and day, night and sunlight display modes.

Benefits

  • One consistent fire record instead of two conflicting ones
  • Unusual fire seasons are visible at a glance
  • Every rating is explained rather than presented as a black box
  • Runs fully offline as a single web page, so it works in the field with no internet

Intended impact
To give researchers, environmental groups and planners fire data they can compare across satellites and years, and to make it easier to spot and prepare for abnormal fire seasons.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: Python (standard library and NumPy) for data processing, the server, the forecast and the spread model; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the interface; Leaflet for maps; SQL and Excel for the baseline dataset; an automated Python test suite
  • SI: Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini Hydrogen Medium
  • Data: NASA FIRMS, MODIS MCD64A1 burned area, MODIS MCD12C1 land cover, the European Commission’s GWIS, Brazil’s INPE Programa Queimadas, and NOAA GSOD weather
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages
  • Hardware: standard laptops only

Creativity
THERMA turns two disagreeing satellite records into one calendar that anyone can read like a heat map of the past decade. The likelihood rating is built only from the historical record, not invented, and the design uses a thermal-camera color palette so the interface itself reads like heat.

Factors we considered

  • Data integrity: we never mix FIRMS and GWIS counts in one baseline, and we flag the faulty November 2025 GWIS counts.
  • Transparency about gaps: missing or suspect data stays visible in the app.
  • Honest limits: the forecast predicts how many hot spots to expect, not where fires will start.
  • Data sources: we used no sources affiliated with China.
  • Usability: offline access, high-contrast sunlight mode and plain-language explanations.
